title: People v. Shaw
description: Whether a gun discovered in an apartment should be suppressed because the defendant's arrest was a "constructive entry" in violation of Payton v New York and the tenant's subsequent consent to search was involuntary or not sufficiently attenuated from the illegal arrest.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued there was no Payton violation as the defendant was arrested outside the apartment and lacked standing to challenge the search, and that the tenant's consent was voluntary and attenuated from any illegality.
defendant_argument: Samuel Shaw argued the gun should be suppressed because his arrest violated Payton due to coercive police tactics constituting a "constructive entry," and the tenant's consent to search was involuntary and not sufficiently attenuated from this illegal arrest.
decision_outcome: The court modified the Appellate Division's order, affirming that the defendant's arrest violated Payton, but remitted the case to the Appellate Division to apply the correct legal standard for determining the voluntariness of the tenant's consent to search, specifically for the charge of criminal possession of a weapon in the second degree (count nine).

title: Clarke v. Town of Newburgh
description: Whether the Town and Town Board of Newburgh, as subordinate governmental entities, can maintain a facial constitutional challenge to the vote dilution provision of the New York Voting Rights Act.
plaintiff_argument: The respondents (Oral Clarke, et al.) argued that Newburgh, as a political subdivision, lacks the capacity to challenge the constitutionality of a state law like the NYVRA, based on long-standing New York legal precedent.
defendant_argument: The appellants (Town of Newburgh, et al.) argued that they can bring a facial constitutional challenge to the NYVRA's vote-dilution provision, claiming that compliance with the statute would force them to violate constitutional equal protection clauses, fitting a narrow 'dilemma' exception.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, holding that Newburgh, as a political subdivision, cannot assert a facial constitutional challenge to the NYVRA's vote-dilution provision because it failed to demonstrate that compliance would force it to violate equal protection.

title: People v. Sargeant
description: Whether a defendant may forfeit the constitutional right to a trial by a jury of 12 persons by engaging in egregious misconduct that requires the discharge of a deliberating juror when no alternate jurors are available.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the defendant forfeited his right to a trial by a jury of 12 by intentionally engaging in egregious misconduct, specifically jury tampering, which resulted in the foreperson's inability to continue serving.
defendant_argument: The defendant declined to waive his right to a trial by a jury of 12 and moved for a mistrial, arguing that continuing with 11 jurors would be inappropriate and that a single act of misconduct should not result in forfeiture of this right.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, concluding that the defendant forfeited his right to a trial by a jury of 12 due to egregious misconduct and that proceeding with the remaining 11 jurors was a proper exercise of the trial court's discretion.

title: Onondaga v. New York
description: Whether the Even Year Election Law (EYEL) is an unconstitutional exercise of legislative authority that violates the home rule provisions of Article IX of the New York State Constitution, as argued by the plaintiffs, or if it is a constitutional and proper exercise of state power aimed at increasing voter participation, as argued by the defendants.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Even Year Election Law (EYEL) is unconstitutional because it violates Article IX of the State Constitution by infringing on counties' constitutional right to set the timing of county elections and terms of office, is not a valid general or special law, and improperly affects existing local legislation.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Even Year Election Law (EYEL) is constitutional, a valid general law, and a proper exercise of legislative authority designed to consolidate local elections with state and federal elections to increase voter turnout and reduce voter confusion.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, ruling that the Even Year Election Law (EYEL) is constitutional and does not violate the New York Constitution.

title: Glen Oaks Village Owners v. City of New York
description: Whether New York City's Local Law No. 97, which aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from large buildings, is preempted by the State's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, with plaintiffs arguing for preemption and defendants arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that Local Law No. 97 is preempted by the Climate Act because the State has occupied the field of regulating greenhouse gas emissions, implying a need for statewide uniformity.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the Climate Act does not preempt Local Law No. 97, as the State Legislature did not express or imply an intent to occupy the entire field and explicitly encouraged complementary local action.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, granting the defendants' motion and holding that the Climate Act does not preempt New York City's Local Law No. 97.

title: Cuomo v. New York State Commission on Ethics and Lobbying in Government
description: Whether the Ethics Commission Reform Act of 2022 unconstitutionally vests the State Commission on Ethics and Lobbying in Government with executive power, with the plaintiff arguing it does so without sufficient gubernatorial oversight and displaces the impeachment process, and the defendant arguing it is constitutional as the Legislature can vest independent bodies with executive power and the Governor's appointment/removal powers are not exclusive.
plaintiff_argument: The Ethics Commission Reform Act of 2022 is facially unconstitutional because it empowers the Commission to exercise executive powers without sufficient oversight by the Governor and unconstitutionally displaces the constitutional impeachment process.
defendant_argument: The Act is constitutional because New York's separation of powers doctrine is flexible, the Governor does not have sole and unlimited powers to appoint or remove state officers, and the Act provides an ethics enforcement mechanism targeted at problems inherent in the Executive Branch's self-regulation to maintain public trust.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the order of the Appellate Division, ruling that the Ethics Commission Reform Act of 2022 is constitutional and does not unconstitutionally encroach upon the powers of the Governor or the Executive Branch.

title: Amedure v. State
description: Whether Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) violates the equal representation mandate in article II, section 8 of the New York Constitution and principles of judicial review.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) violates the equal representation mandate by allowing a ballot to be processed as valid even with a split board decision, and improperly restricts judicial review, potentially enabling electoral fraud.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) is constitutional, secures equal representation, and does not unconstitutionally constrain the judiciary, as sufficient safeguards against fraud exist.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) does not violate the constitutional principles of equal representation, separation of powers, or judicial review.

title: Fossella v. Adams
description: Whether Local Law 11, which allows non-citizens to vote in New York City municipal elections, is constitutional, with plaintiffs arguing it violates the State Constitution's restriction of voting to citizens and defendants arguing it is a lawful exercise of home rule authority.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argued that Local Law 11, which allows non-citizens to vote in municipal elections, violates Article II, Section 1 of the New York State Constitution (limiting voting to citizens), the New York State Election Law, and the Municipal Home Rule Law (requiring a public referendum for changes to voting methods).
defendant_argument: Defendants (City Council, Mayor, BOE, and intervenors) argued that Local Law 11 is a lawful exercise of home rule authority under Article IX of the State Constitution, which allows localities to expand the franchise, and that Article II, Section 1 merely sets a floor for voting rights, not a ceiling.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Local Law 11 is null and void because the New York State Constitution restricts voting to citizens, thereby affirming the Appellate Division's decision.

title: Stefanik v. Hochul
description: Whether New York's Early Mail Voter Act, which permits all registered voters to vote early by mail, violates the New York Constitution by allowing voting methods beyond those historically understood or explicitly permitted.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Early Mail Voter Act is unconstitutional because the New York Constitution historically mandated in-person voting and limits absentee voting to specific circumstances, and a recent ballot initiative to allow universal mail-in voting was rejected by voters.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Act is constitutional, as the Constitution does not explicitly prohibit mail-in voting, especially after the 1966 amendment removed the in-person voting requirement, and the legislature has broad powers to regulate elections.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, ruling that New York's Early Mail Voter Act is constitutional and does not violate the State Constitution.

title: People v. Watkins
description: Whether trial counsel was constitutionally ineffective for failing to request a cross-racial identification instruction at the close of the trial.
plaintiff_argument: The People (respondent) argued that trial counsel was not ineffective because, at the time of Watkins' trial, such an instruction was discretionary, not mandatory, and thus counsel's failure to request it did not constitute an egregious single error of ineffective assistance.
defendant_argument: Mark Watkins (appellant) argued that his trial counsel was constitutionally ineffective for failing to request a cross-racial identification instruction, especially given the cross-racial nature of the identification and the widely understood importance of such charges.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, upholding Mark Watkins' conviction.

title: People v. Debellis
description: Whether Anthony Debellis received ineffective assistance of counsel when his attorney failed to request a jury instruction on the statutory defense of voluntary surrender for criminal possession of a weapon, with the plaintiff arguing counsel was not ineffective and the defendant arguing counsel was ineffective.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that defense counsel provided meaningful representation and the defendant was not entitled to a voluntary surrender instruction, thus his conviction should stand.
defendant_argument: Anthony Debellis argued that his counsel was ineffective for failing to request a jury instruction on the statutory defense of voluntary surrender, which was supported by his testimony, instead pursuing a meritless defense.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order and ordered a new trial for Anthony Debellis.

title: People v. Rodriguez
description: Whether police interference with a bicyclist constitutes a seizure under federal and state constitutions, requiring reasonable suspicion of a criminal offense or probable cause of a Vehicle and Traffic Law violation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (defendant in the original case) argued that the police stop was an unlawful seizure because the officers lacked reasonable suspicion of criminal activity or probable cause of a traffic violation, and therefore the recovered gun and his statements should be suppressed.
defendant_argument: The defendant (The People) argued that the police encounter was a justified common-law inquiry, not a seizure, or that the officers had sufficient 'founded suspicion' for the stop.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, granted the defendant's motion to suppress the gun and statements, and dismissed the indictment, ruling that a police stop of a bicyclist is a seizure requiring reasonable suspicion or probable cause.

title: Hoffmann v. New York State Independent Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) has a continuing constitutional duty to prepare and submit new legislative redistricting plans for future elections, or if the court-drawn maps from the 2022 election are the exclusive and decade-long remedy.
plaintiff_argument: The IRC has a continuing constitutional duty to prepare and submit a second redistricting plan, even though the 2022 congressional map was judicially adopted, because the court-drawn maps were only an interim remedy for the 2022 election.
defendant_argument: The IRC's deadline to submit a second redistricting plan passed on February 28, 2022, making any current attempt to compel them unconstitutional and untimely, and the court-ordered redistricting plan from Harkenrider is the exclusive remedy that should remain in effect until the 2030 census.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, compelling the Independent Redistricting Commission to reconvene and submit a second redistricting plan and implementing legislation by February 28, 2024.

title: Police Benevolent Association v. City of New York
description: Whether section 10-181 of the Administrative Code of the City of New York, which criminalizes the use of certain restraints by police officers during an arrest, violates the New York Constitution on either preemption or due process grounds.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the local law is unconstitutional because it is preempted by state laws governing police arrest authority and is void for vagueness, particularly regarding the compression of an arrestee's diaphragm, failing to provide adequate notice of prohibited conduct.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the local law is a proper exercise of its home rule authority, is not preempted by state law, and is not vague because police officers receive training on the prohibited conduct.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Administrative Code § 10-181 is constitutional and is neither preempted by state law nor void for vagueness.

title: Stevens v. New York State Division of Criminal Justice Services
description: Whether the legislature's grant of rulemaking authority to the Commission on Forensic Sciences was sufficient to authorize the Commission's promulgation of the Familial DNA Search Regulations.
plaintiff_argument: The Commission lacked the statutory authority to promulgate Familial DNA Search Regulations, which are arbitrary and capricious, and infringe on privacy, particularly for African-Americans, thus violating the separation of powers doctrine.
defendant_argument: The Commission had the statutory authority to promulgate the Familial DNA Search Regulations, which were a proper exercise of its delegated power and not arbitrary or capricious.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order and dismissed the petition, ruling that the Commission had the statutory authority to promulgate the Familial DNA Search Regulations.

title: People v. Regan
description: Whether the excessive preindictment delay by the prosecution violated the defendant's constitutional right to prompt prosecution.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the four-year preindictment delay, while "excessive," was not due to bad faith and did not cause actual prejudice to the defendant, therefore not violating his due process rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the excessive preindictment delay of over four years violated his constitutional due process right to prompt prosecution, warranting dismissal of the indictment.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order and dismissed the indictment, ruling in favor of the defendant.

title: Owner Operator Independent Drivers Association v. NYS Department of Transportation
description: Whether New York regulations requiring electronic logging devices (ELDs) in commercial motor vehicles and authorizing warrantless inspections of ELD data violate the State Constitution's protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that New York's ELD rule, which mandates warrantless inspections of ELD data, constitutes an unreasonable search and seizure under the State Constitution and fails to adequately limit the frequency of such searches.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the ELD rule's warrantless inspections fall under the administrative search exception to the warrant requirement for pervasively regulated industries and are constitutional under the State Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the New York regulations adopting the ELD rule, which authorizes warrantless inspections, are facially constitutional and do not violate the State Constitution's protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.

title: St. Lawrence Cnty. v. City of Ogdensburg
description: Whether Local Law No. 2-2021 of City of Ogdensburg, which repealed a prior local law opting out of the application of Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) article 11, is inconsistent with RPTL 1150 or otherwise unconstitutional under the home rule article of the New York State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, St. Lawrence County, argued that Local Law No. 2 was inconsistent with RPTL 1150 and impaired the County's powers by unlawfully shifting the burden of enforcing and collecting delinquent City and School District taxes without an agreement, violating the New York Constitution and Municipal Home Rule Law.
defendant_argument: The defendant, City of Ogdensburg, argued that Local Law No. 2 is valid and enforceable because RPTL article 11 allows a city to opt back in by repealing its prior opt-out law, and RPTL 1102 (6)(b) supports a county enforcing delinquent taxes for a city via its charter without requiring a special procedure or agreement under RPTL 1150.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Local Law No. 2 is not inconsistent with RPTL 1150 or unconstitutional, and that it properly effectuates a power granted to cities to revoke their initial opt-out from RPTL article 11.

title: People v. Johnson
description: Whether the police had reasonable suspicion to justify a level three stop and frisk of Tyquan Johnson under the De Bour framework, with the plaintiff arguing that the police action was justified and the defendant arguing it was not.
plaintiff_argument: The police action, including the stop and frisk, was justified at its inception and at every subsequent stage of the encounter leading to Mr. Johnson's arrest, based on his movements and appearance.
defendant_argument: The police lacked the requisite level of suspicion to justify an intrusion under any level of the De Bour framework, specifically that his actions did not constitute reasonable suspicion for a level three stop and frisk.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the police lacked reasonable suspicion for the stop and frisk, and dismissed the indictment against Tyquan Johnson.

title: Delgado v. State
description: Whether the enabling act, which created a committee to determine salaries for state officials, constituted an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority, with plaintiffs arguing it did and defendants arguing it did not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the enabling act unconstitutionally delegated legislative authority to the Committee and violated the constitutional requirement that legislative salaries be "fixed by law".
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the enabling act was a valid assignment of power to the Committee, operating within constitutional limits, and that the plaintiffs failed to overcome the presumption of constitutionality.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the enabling act had not been shown to be unconstitutional.

title: Harkenrider v. Hochul
description: Whether the legislature's 2022 congressional and state senate redistricting maps are unconstitutional due to procedural failures by the Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) and the legislature, and due to unconstitutional partisan gerrymandering.
plaintiff_argument: The legislature's redistricting maps were unconstitutionally enacted because the IRC failed to submit a second redistricting plan as required, and the congressional map was unconstitutionally gerrymandered to favor the majority party.
defendant_argument: Petitioners lacked standing, the IRC's failure did not strip the legislature of its authority to enact redistricting plans, and petitioners failed to prove the maps were unconstitutionally partisan.
decision_outcome: The court declared the congressional and state senate maps void due to procedural unconstitutionality and substantive partisan gerrymandering, and remitted the case to the Supreme Court for new maps to be drawn with the assistance of a special master.

title: People v. Dawson
description: Whether Malik Dawson unequivocally invoked his right to counsel during police interrogation, with the plaintiff arguing his request was equivocal and the defendant arguing it was unequivocal.
plaintiff_argument: The defendant's inquiries and demeanor suggested only a conditional interest in speaking with an attorney, and he did not unequivocally invoke his right to counsel, thus his waiver of Miranda rights was valid.
defendant_argument: Malik Dawson unequivocally and repeatedly asked to contact his lawyer, and therefore his subsequent waiver of Miranda rights without counsel present was invalid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, upholding the conviction and the finding that the defendant did not unequivocally invoke his right to counsel.

title: White v. Cuomo
description: Whether Interactive Fantasy Sports (IFS) contests constitute unlawful "gambling" under Article I, § 9 of the New York Constitution, which prohibits unauthorized gambling.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that IFS contests involve a material degree of chance and are essentially bets or wagers on future contingent events outside participants' control, thus constituting prohibited gambling under the State Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that IFS contests are skill-based competitions where participants exercise substantial influence over the outcome through knowledge and strategy, and therefore do not fall under the constitutional prohibition against gambling.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Article 14 of the Racing, Pari-Mutuel Wagering and Breeding Law, which authorizes IFS contests, does not violate the New York Constitution's prohibition on gambling.

title: People v. Torres
description: Whether the New York City Right of Way Law, which imposes criminal liability based on ordinary negligence for drivers who injure pedestrians or bicyclists, violates due process or is preempted by state law.
plaintiff_argument: The People of the State of New York argued that the Right of Way Law is constitutional, that ordinary negligence is a sufficient mens rea for criminal liability, and that the law is not preempted by state law, falling within the City's delegated authority to regulate traffic.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Right of Way Law is unconstitutional because its ordinary negligence mens rea violates due process and that it is preempted by state law, specifically the Penal Law regarding culpable mental states and the Vehicle and Traffic Law regarding traffic infractions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Term's decision, rejecting the defendants' constitutional challenges and upholding the validity of the Right of Way Law.

title: People v. Schneider
description: Whether a Kings County Supreme Court Justice had jurisdiction to issue eavesdropping warrants for defendant's cell phones, which were not physically present in New York, for the purpose of gathering evidence in an investigation of enterprise corruption and gambling offenses committed in Kings County.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that eavesdropping warrants are executed in the geographical jurisdiction where law enforcement officers intentionally intercept communications, regardless of the physical location of the cell phones or call participants, and that this interpretation ensures proper oversight.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Kings County Supreme Court Justice lacked authority to issue the eavesdropping warrants because his cell phones and call participants were not located in New York, meaning the warrants were not 'executed' in Kings County as required by law, and that this constituted an unconstitutional extraterritorial application of New York law.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's judgment, ruling that the Kings County Supreme Court Justice had jurisdiction to issue the eavesdropping warrants.

title: Protect the Adirondacks! Inc. v. New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
description: Whether the state's plan for constructing approximately 27 miles of Class II community connector trails for snowmobile use in the Forest Preserve is permissible under the New York Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it violates the "forever wild" provision by requiring substantial timber destruction and the defendant arguing it is permissible as it balances protection and public access without substantially impairing the wild forest nature.
plaintiff_argument: The construction of snowmobile trails, involving the cutting and removal of thousands of trees, grading, and leveling, violates the "forever wild" provision of the New York State Constitution (art XIV, § 1) and creates an artificial man-made setting.
defendant_argument: The planned snowmobile trails are permissible as they balance protecting the Forest Preserve with allowing year-round access, do not substantially impair the wild forest nature, and are similar to existing trails.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, holding that the planned construction of the Class II community connector trails would violate the New York State Constitution's "forever wild" provision.

title: People v. Gordon
description: Whether a search warrant authorizing the search of "entire premises" implicitly permits the search of vehicles located on those premises, even if the vehicles are not specifically mentioned in the warrant.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that a warrant to search an "entire premises" may impliedly authorize a search of automobiles found on the property, relying on federal caselaw that treats vehicles as containers.
defendant_argument: Mr. Gordon argued that police lacked particularized probable cause to search the vehicles because the warrant did not specifically mention them, nor did the warrant application provide probable cause for searching the vehicles.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' decision to suppress the physical evidence seized from the two vehicles, ruling that the search warrant did not authorize the search of the vehicles.
